nameStory: Sweet everlasting gets its name from two wonderful qualities: the maple syrup-like fragrance it releases when you crush its leaves, and its papery flowers that keep their color and shape long after drying. The 'everlasting' part made it popular for dried flower arrangements that would stay beautiful through winter when fresh blooms were impossible to find.
description: Sweet everlasting is a soft, fuzzy annual plant that grows 1-3 feet tall in sunny, sandy spots throughout New England. It has narrow, woolly leaves that feel almost cottony to the touch and clusters of small, papery white flowers that appear from late summer into fall. The whole plant has a silvery-green appearance due to its dense covering of fine white hairs, giving it an almost ghostly look in bright sunlight.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves covered in dense white woolly hairs that make them feel soft and cottony. When you crush them, they release a distinctive sweet maple syrup scent that's unmistakable.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white to yellowish flowers clustered in dense, flat-topped groups at the plant's tip. Each flower head feels papery and dry, almost like tissue paper, even when fresh.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright annual, 1-3 feet tall, often forming loose colonies in disturbed areas. The whole plant appears silvery-green due to its fuzzy white coating.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are covered in the same dense white woolly hairs as the leaves, feeling soft and almost velvety when you run your fingers along them.

habitat: Sweet everlasting thrives in open, dry, sandy soils throughout New England, especially in old fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas. You'll often find it growing alongside goldenrod, wild asters, and other late-season wildflowers in sunny spots where the soil drains well. It's particularly common in coastal areas and inland sandy plains.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in spring, but young plants are small and easily overlooked among other emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow steadily through summer, developing their characteristic woolly leaves and silvery appearance, but flowers haven't appeared yet.
seasonality.fall: This is prime time for sweet everlasting, when the distinctive papery white flower clusters appear and the maple syrup scent is strongest in crushed leaves.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried flower heads still attached, maintaining their papery white appearance even under snow.

funFact: Sweet everlasting was traditionally smoked by some Native American tribes and early European settlers as a tobacco substitute, earning it the nickname 'rabbit tobacco' - though despite the name, it's completely unrelated to actual tobacco and belongs to the daisy family instead!
confusionNotes: Sweet everlasting might be confused with other fuzzy white plants like mullein or lamb's ear, but the distinctive maple syrup scent when crushed and the papery flower clusters are dead giveaways. Remember: if it smells like pancake breakfast, you've found your everlasting!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'rabbit tobacco,' this plant is actually in the daisy and sunflower family (Asteraceae), not related to true tobacco at all. The name comes from its historical use as a smoking herb, while 'rabbit' likely refers to the soft, fuzzy texture that resembles rabbit fur.
compareHints: Sweet everlasting differs from its close relative Macoun's everlasting mainly in its preferred habitat and leaf shape - sweet everlasting has narrower leaves and grows in drier, sandier spots, while Macoun's everlasting prefers moister areas and has slightly broader leaves. Both share the characteristic woolly texture and papery flowers, but sweet everlasting is much more commonly encountered in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Macoun's everlasting differs from its close relative sweet everlasting by having narrower, more linear leaves and a more openly branched flower arrangement.
